claims.text: A thin amorphous alumina coating deposited by ALD suppresses surface diffusion in Al0.1CrCoFeNi nanoalloys at 700–900 K.
Suppressing surface diffusion with the coating mitigates high-temperature surface segregation.
The alumina coating preserves chemical homogeneity relative to uncoated Al0.1CrCoFeNi nanoalloys.
The alumina coating preserves lattice integrity relative to uncoated Al0.1CrCoFeNi nanoalloys.
The as-synthesized Al0.1CrCoFeNi nanoalloys have a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
The amorphous alumina layer reduces the surface energy of the nanoalloy.
Reduced surface energy significantly limits surface-atom mobility at high temperature.
Atomic rearrangements in Al0.1CrCoFeNi can produce clustering or local chemical ordering.
Limiting surface-atom mobility prevents the rearrangements that cause surface segregation and local chemical ordering.
Coated nanoalloys will retain uniform chemical composition up to 900 K.
Coated nanoalloys will retain stable lattice parameters with minimal diffraction-peak shifts up to 900 K.
Annealed uncoated Al0.1CrCoFeNi nanoalloys will exhibit clustering or segregation.
Annealed uncoated samples will show diffraction changes associated with segregation.
The prediction is restricted to 700–900 K.
The prediction may not apply under reactive atmospheric conditions.
The coating effect is expected in nanoalloys having compositional homogeneity similar to the studied system.
Coating-induced mechanical stress or interfacial reactions may influence the observed stability.
Similar post-annealing segregation, chemical inhomogeneity, and lattice shifts in coated and uncoated samples would falsify the hypothesis.
